title: Switching On Ras Without Touching It

scenes.tts: A growth factor binds its receptor, and Ras switches on. Yet the receptor never touches Ras. Ras is a small switch protein, anchored to the inner face of the plasma membrane. The receptor adds phosphates to tyrosines on its own tail. A phosphate on a tail is a message written where nothing can read it yet, so what sits in between?
scenes.visual: Membrane across the top, a receptor bar with a three-tyrosine tail on the left, Ras hanging under the membrane on the right. A growth factor lands; Ras flashes on; a red line shows the receptor never touches Ras; phosphates run down the tail; a dashed path of question marks fills the gap.
scenes.caption: A growth factor binds its receptor, and Ras switches on. Yet the receptor never touches Ras. Ras is a small switch protein, anchored to the inner face of the plasma membrane. The receptor adds phosphates to tyrosines on its own tail. A phosphate on a tail is a message written where nothing can read it yet, so what sits in between?

The receptor adds phosphates to tyrosines on its own tail. A phosphate on a tail is a message written where nothing can read it yet, so what sits in between?

scenes.tts: Each phosphorylated tyrosine on the tail is a handhold for proteins that carry an S H 2 domain. An S H 2 domain is a small folded module, and it grips a phosphorylated tyrosine. The cell passes the message on by recruiting these proteins. Some of the proteins that arrive are enzymes. Others have no enzyme activity, and only decide who stands next to whom.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the tail. A cup (the SH2 domain) closes on a phosphate. Two proteins carrying a cup arrive: one is labelled enzyme, one no enzyme activity, with a partner standing beside it.
scenes.caption: Each phosphorylated tyrosine on the tail is a handhold for proteins that carry an SH2 domain. An SH2 domain is a small folded module, and it grips a phosphorylated tyrosine. The cell passes the message on by recruiting these proteins. Some of the proteins that arrive are enzymes. Others have no enzyme activity, and only decide who stands next to whom.
scenes.narration: Each phosphorylated tyrosine on the tail is a handhold for proteins that carry an SH2 domain. An SH2 domain is a small folded module, and it grips a phosphorylated tyrosine. The cell passes the message on by recruiting these proteins. Some of the proteins that arrive are enzymes. Others have no enzyme activity, and only decide who stands next to whom.

scenes.tts: One of those proteins, the one with no enzyme activity at all, is Grab two. It has one S H 2 domain, two S H 3 domains, and nothing else. An S H 3 domain is another small module that grips short stretches rich in proline. Its two S H 3 domains already hold a protein called S O S, with or without any phosphate. Only the S H 2 domain needs a phosphate.
scenes.visual: The no-enzyme protein is named Grb2, lets go of the tail, and the view closes in: one SH2 cup, two SH3 claws gripping the partner, which grows into Sos. A phosphate visits the claws (nothing changes), then the cup (it closes).
scenes.caption: One of those proteins, the one with no enzyme activity at all, is Grb2. It has one SH2 domain, two SH3 domains, and nothing else. An SH3 domain is another small module that grips short stretches rich in proline. Its two SH3 domains already hold a protein called Sos, with or without any phosphate. Only the SH2 domain needs a phosphate.

An SH3 domain is another small module that grips short stretches rich in proline. Its two SH3 domains already hold a protein called Sos, with or without any phosphate. Only the SH2 domain needs a phosphate.

scenes.tts: Now the S H 2 domain of Grab two clamps down on a phosphotyrosine on the receptor tail. So the receptor holds Grab two, and Grab two holds S O S. S O S now stands at the membrane, where Ras is. So one phosphotyrosine on the tail ends up positioning S O S next to Ras. Position does the rest.
scenes.visual: Grb2, holding Sos, slides to the tail and the cup clamps the phosphate. A ring marks each hold. Ras stands against the top of Sos, and the holds light up in order from the phosphate to Ras.
scenes.caption: Now the SH2 domain of Grb2 clamps down on a phosphotyrosine on the receptor tail. So the receptor holds Grb2, and Grb2 holds Sos. Sos now stands at the membrane, where Ras is. So one phosphotyrosine on the tail ends up positioning Sos next to Ras. Position does the rest.

scenes.tts: S O S has one task here. It is an exchange factor that swaps the G D P on Ras for G T P. That flips Ras from off to on, and no kinase is involved. Grab two never grips Ras at all. It only holds S O S, which acts on Ras.
scenes.visual: Sos is named an exchange factor. The GDP tag on Ras is swapped for GTP and Ras turns green. A kinase is crossed out, and so is any direct line from Grb2 to Ras.
scenes.caption: Sos has one task here. It is an exchange factor that swaps the GDP on Ras for GTP. That flips Ras from off to on, and no kinase is involved. Grb2 never grips Ras at all. It only holds Sos, which acts on Ras.
scenes.narration: Sos has one task here. It is an exchange factor that swaps the GDP on Ras for GTP. That flips Ras from off to on, and no kinase is involved. Grb2 never grips Ras at all. It only holds Sos, which acts on Ras.

scenes.tts: The receptor never touched Ras. Grab two clamped a phosphate on the tail, with S O S already in its grip. S O S then flipped Ras from off to on. Grab two is called an adaptor: it has no enzyme activity, and it links two partners. Keep this rule: the receptor holds Grab two, Grab two holds S O S, and position does the rest.
scenes.visual: The red gap line again: the receptor never touched Ras. Grb2 is labelled adaptor, with two partners; then a ring lights each hold in turn: receptor to Grb2, Grb2 to Sos, Sos against Ras.
